newsitem.title: BOSNIA: International community appeals to Bosnia's voters.
newsitem.headline: International community appeals to Bosnia's voters.

text.p: International leaders, rejecting accusations they were leading Bosnia to partition, appealed to its people on Friday to vote for peace and reconciliation in general elections on Saturday.

U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke, architect of the Dayton peace accords which ended the war, said the polls would pave the way for the next stage of the peace process -- creation of central government structures.

"The Dayton agreement does not provide for secession. We are opposed to that and we all agree that that is not what this election is all about," he told reporters after a meeting with Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic.
State television later said Izetbegovic, a Moslem, had assured Holbrooke his government had taken all the steps it could to make sure the polls passed off peacefully.

Holbrooke said some candidates had adopted public positions calling for separatism, secession, racist attitudes, ethnic division and "all things Americans abhor and were banned in the Dayton accords".
"They can say anything they want in a country supposed to respect freedom of speech, but they are signatories of Dayton which does not provide for that," he added.

U.S. Admiral Joseph Lopez, commander of 60,000 NATO peace troops, international peace coordinator Carl Bildt, and Robert Frowick, who is overseeing the elections as regional director of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe also urged Bosnians to vote for peace in a joint statement.

"We urge you all to approach election day with dignity, to consider your own choice carefully, and to know that your vote is a secret vote," they urged Bosnia's Moslems, Serbs and Croats who have scant experience with democracy.
They said authorities in Bosnia's estranged Moslem, Serb and Croat-dominated ethnic entities had cooperated well to create conditions for voting in peace and security.
"We urge you to support their and our efforts. We will react with determination against any acts of manipulation or provocation," Lopez, Bildt and Frowick said.
"Tomorrow, the eyes of the world will be on Bosnia and on all of you. This is your day to show your national desire for peace, and your own personal and secret choice for a better future."

Voters will be choosing a multi-ethnic three-person presidency and united parliament, regional assemblies in Moslem-Croat Federation and Serb Republic entities, and cantonal councils in the Federation.

Ethnic nationalist campaigning by the three main parties have raised fears that the elections will only seal Bosnia's division wrought by war as Moslems, Serbs and Croats deadlock over power-sharing arrangements.
Bildt told Reuters the longer elections were delayed the more difficult reconciliation would be to achieve.

"I think we have delayed the process too long because we need to set up the common institutions and the longer that process is delayed the more difficult will it be to overcome the partition of the country," he said.
